title: Computer & workstation foundations
summary: How computers run programs, files/paths, data representation, problem solving, a working Linux+Git+uv workstation, a study system and the algebra you need — all with real resources (CS50x L0, Crash Course CS, Software Carpentry, Microsoft/uv docs, Khan Academy).

units.title: How a computer runs a program
outcomes: You can explain the journey of a program from disk to RAM to CPU.
You can tell a process from a program and read one in Task Manager / htop.
You can explain why GPUs suit AI workloads and estimate a model's memory from its parameter count.

learn.title: The Central Processing Unit (CPU): Crash Course Computer Science #7
learn.slice: Crash Course CS #7 'The Central Processing Unit (CPU)' (full episode, ~12 min); then #8 'Instructions & Programs', #18 'Operating Systems', #19 'Memory & Storage' (each ~10-13 min)

covers: CPU fetch-decode-execute cycle, registers, clock speed (#7)
Machine instructions and how a program is a sequence of them (#8)
What an operating system does: scheduling, memory protection, device drivers, processes (#18)
RAM vs persistent storage (HDD/SSD), volatility, memory hierarchy (#19)

practice.title: Inspect your own machine
practice.brief: Open Task Manager (Windows) or `htop` (WSL/Linux). Write `how-my-computer-works.md` (½ page): name 3 running processes and their RAM, your RAM vs disk size, and compute why a 7B-parameter model needs ~14 GB at fp16 (2 bytes/param).
practice.done_when: File committed with 3 processes + RAM figures, disk/RAM sizes and the 7B×2 bytes = 14 GB calculation explained in your own words.

quiz.prompt: Data that survives a reboot lives in:
quiz.explain: RAM, caches and registers are volatile; disk/SSD is persistent storage (Crash Course #19).

quiz.prompt: A running instance of a program is a:
quiz.explain: The OS loads the program into memory and runs it as a process with its own address space (Crash Course #18).

options: Many identical arithmetic operations in parallel
quiz.explain: GPUs have thousands of simple cores built for the same arithmetic on many values (matrix maths), which is what neural nets are.

quiz.prompt: A 7B-parameter model stored in fp16 needs roughly:
quiz.explain: fp16 = 2 bytes per parameter, so 7e9 × 2 B ≈ 14 GB (before activations/KV cache).

quiz.prompt: Explain what happens, at the level of disk → RAM → CPU → OS, when you double-click a program.
rubric: Program file is read from disk into RAM by the OS
OS creates a process (memory space, scheduling)
CPU fetches/decodes/executes instructions from RAM
Mentions that RAM is volatile / disk persistent

practice.title: Working-directory experiment
practice.brief: In WSL (or cs50.dev), write the absolute and relative path from `~/code/a/b` to `~/data/x.csv`. Create `script.py` that does `open('x.csv')`; run it from two different directories and explain why it fails in one. Fix it with `Path(__file__).parent / 'x.csv'`.
practice.done_when: `paths.md` committed with both paths, the failing + working command lines, and a 3-sentence explanation.

quiz.explain: Relative paths are resolved from the process's current working directory, not the script's location.

quiz.prompt: An absolute path on Linux starts with:
quiz.explain: `/` is the root; `~` is a shell shortcut that expands to an absolute home path.

options: How programs choose to interpret the file
quiz.explain: Extensions are naming conventions; the content is unchanged.

options: The editor edits source text; the terminal runs programs (including Python on that source)
quiz.explain: Source code is text you edit; execution happens when an interpreter runs it, usually started from a terminal.

quiz.prompt: Why does 'it works on my machine' so often come down to the working directory?
rubric: Relative paths resolve against cwd
Different launch locations (IDE vs terminal) give different cwd
Fix: build paths from __file__ or pass absolute paths/config

practice.title: Represent things by hand and in Python
practice.brief: By hand convert 5, 50, 255 to binary and hex. In Python print `'é'.encode('utf-8')`, `len('😀'.encode('utf-8'))`, `0.1 + 0.2`, and `hex(255)`; explain each output in `data-rep.md`.
practice.done_when: All four outputs shown and explained; hand conversions correct (255 = 0b11111111 = 0xff).

quiz.explain: A byte is 8 bits, 256 possible values.
UTF-8 is ASCII-compatible: code points < 128 use one byte; others use 2–4.

options: False, because of binary floating point
quiz.explain: 0.1 has no exact binary representation, so the sum is 0.30000000000000004.

quiz.prompt: Why can an emoji take more bytes than a letter, and why does that matter when you count 'characters' for an LLM?
rubric: UTF-8 is variable-length; emoji code points need 4 bytes
len(str) counts code points, len(bytes) counts bytes
LLMs count tokens, which are built from bytes/subwords, not characters
So cost/limits differ from character counts

practice.title: Pseudocode → trace → debug
practice.brief: Write pseudocode for 'find the cheapest item in a list'. Trace it by hand on [5, 3, 9] in a table (step, variable values). Paste a deliberately broken Python version into Python Tutor and write down what the last traceback line says.
practice.done_when: `trace.md` committed: pseudocode, a full trace table, the traceback's last line quoted and explained.

options: Splitting a problem into smaller sub-problems
quiz.explain: Decomposition breaks a task into parts you can solve and test separately.

quiz.prompt: In a Python traceback, the most specific error is usually on:
quiz.explain: Python prints the call stack oldest-first; the exception type and message are on the last line.

quiz.prompt: `True and False or True` evaluates to:
quiz.explain: `and` binds tighter: (True and False) = False; False or True = True.
Tracing means stepping through by hand, writing each variable's value at each step.

quiz.prompt: Describe a bug you hit this week and what the error message actually told you.
rubric: Names the exception type
Identifies the line/cause the message pointed to
Explains the fix
Notes what they'd check first next time

Exit code 0 means success; non-zero means failure.

practice.title: Set up your study system
practice.brief: Create `learning-log.md` (daily: studied / built / confused me / card added) and `mistakes.md`. Install Anki and add 15 cards from Week 1. Write your AI-use policy in 5 rules (e.g. 'AI may explain; I never paste code I can't re-derive').
practice.done_when: Log has ≥5 daily entries, Anki shows ≥15 cards, policy committed to `foundations` repo.

quiz.prompt: The most effective revision technique here is:
quiz.explain: Retrieval practice strengthens memory far more than rereading.
Intervals grow each time you recall correctly.

options: Be the smallest code that still shows the bug
quiz.explain: Small, runnable, with the exact error text.

quiz.prompt: When is using an AI assistant harmful to learning, even if the code works?
rubric: When it replaces the struggle that builds the skill
When you can't explain/re-derive the code
Mentions a rule they will follow (e.g. attempt first, then ask for hints)

capstone.title: My machine, explained
capstone.brief: (3h) Public GitHub repo `foundations` containing: setup-log.md with verify.py output and exit 0; how-my-computer-works.md (disk→RAM→CPU, process, path); a hand-traced algorithm; the binary/hex/UTF-8/float exercise; Khan unit-test screenshots; learning log + ≥30 Anki cards + AI policy. Pass at ≥7/10 with no zero on the toolchain row.

rubric.criterion: Toolchain works (verify.py exits 0; git, uv, python run from WSL)
Concept accuracy (process, RAM vs disk, paths)
Learning system (log, ≥30 Anki cards, AI policy)
